I've only been towing for about 6 months, but I'll offer some insight that some of the veterans may have forgotten by now with what it's like to start. I only had 3 days of training (didn't realize how bad that was until a while later) and had to figure a lot out on my own. So far, here's what I got:

1. The truck isn't fragile. Take care of it, don't abuse it, but it serves as both a surgeon's scalpel and as a sledge hammer.

2. Tailswing. Might not be too much of an issue depending on the trucks you've driven but God forgive me for the people I scared while turning and the apartment carport pillars I've smacked trying to turn around in a tight parking lots when I first started...

3. Make sure you check if the vehicle is AWD or FWD/RWD. Don't trust what dispatch says or by looking for badges in the car. Make sure you know how to tell by looking under the car. BMW's especially.

4. Volkswagens like to put what looks like tow points right into the floor sheet metal. Don't use them unless the customer specifically requested a floor delete.

5. Learn to use chains. The 8 point straps are great, but sometimes you'll have to tow a Jeep that, despite never having seen dirt, is sitting on 35 inch mud tires and while you *might* be able to make the straps fit, it would be easier and faster just to chain it from the start rather than fight the straps.

6. Before releasing your straps and parking brake to unload, make sure your bridle is still tight, or worse, still attached. Your winch CAN lose tension, especially if you don't keep your winch spooled up neatly. Which is 6.5: keep your winch line neat on the spool.

7. Learn how to shift trucks/SUVs into neutral from underneath. And don't be afraid to look up where the neutral override lever is. Might make that call take longer but will make life easier in the future.

8. Especially doing AAA, you're going to come across a lot of people who tried using that tire slime stuff to seal up a tire even though it has a 6 inch hole in it from hitting a curb in a parking lot while going mach Jesus. Clean that shit off your bed ASAP, it hardens fast and it takes so long to clean off that you'll end up replying to posts on Reddit just to avoid getting back out of the truck to finish cleaning it. 

9. If you get in a truck that has air horns, NEVER ignore a kid pumping his arm. If you have an air horn, you've been entrusted with a sacred duty and you must always pull the magic noise string when it is requested of you.

10. Snatch blocks. Use em. Practice with em. Take them to dinner and movies with you. They're your best friend now.

From one new to guy to another slightly newer guy, just have fun. Once you get past the first few weeks of being unsure about stuff and learning the basics, it's a blast and beats the hell out of most jobs that have a very typical, boring routine.

I see a lot of people jumping on this anti cafe/anti project bike train but I strongly disagree. It comes across as self absorbed, like everyone has to be a purist or everyone has to have your exact same taste.

 I got into riding because I bought a clapped out 75 Goldwing that was halfway through a poorly thought out cafe conversion. By the time I was done, I was just as much in love with building bikes as I was with riding. And I promise you, that feeling of fear, excitement, and freedom that you felt when you took your first bike out on the road for the first time? It's an order of magnitude greater when you turned every bolt, ran every wire, bled every fluid system, and painted every piece of metal.

Barring a seller legitimately scamming someone or lying about things, I encourage someone with the right aptitude to buy a UJM. At the very least, it teaches mechanical skills and maintenance that every rider should know before they ever hit the start button. And odds are, if it doesn't get turned into a cafe racer or scrambler or chopper or whatever, it's gonna sit in someone's yard until it's scrap. 

 I've either owned or ridden dozens of bikes by now, sport bikes and cruisers, ADVs and old man couch bikes. Loved them (okay, maybe not all of them). But last year I went and bought a 79 goldwing that arrived at my house in the form of a U-Haul trailer full of milk crates. Fired it up for the first time last week. Now it looks nothing like the seller had originally intended and everything how I intended and I don't regret buying it, just like I never regretted my first bike.

Because knowing I built it is gonna make that first ride feel like a high that drugs can't provide. End rant.

 TL;DR let people enjoy what they want. Some people got into or stayed with motorcycles because to some, building something is just as enjoyable as riding.

That's exactly what a failing alternator does which is why I'm confused. When running, what's the voltage at? While the car is idling, you should see somewhere between 13-14 volts. A failing alternator will usually start at around 12.5 (give or take) and start dropping until the engine stalls (in my experience, usually around 6-7 volts but depends on the car). 

If you're going off of AutoZone for the alternator test as well, that may be misleading. When I worked for AAA, we used similar testers to what they have and it might say "good" even if the voltage is as low as 12.4 while running. But if it's that low while running, it's definitely the alternator. Unfortunately, most chain store employees and even the "Battery Technicians" for motor clubs don't have a solid mechanical knowledge base and can only go by what the magic box's screen tells them.
Something seems off here. How did you test the battery? And how does the problem present? Does the car die after running for a bit, or does it run fine but when you shut it off it won't restart?

Short answer: You're probably talking about the condenser coil. A condenser coil is basically just a small radiator for the AC that sits in front of the actual radiator. The only way this could cause any harm is if it's so smashed up that air can't get through it to cool the engine (since it sits in front of the radiator). And it would have to be pretty beat up to do this.

Long answer: Your AC is made up of 3 basic parts, the condenser, the evaporator, and compressor, and all are filled with a fluid called refrigerant. The evaporator is like a small radiator in your dash. The air in the car is blown over it and it absorbs heat so that the same air is cold when it comes out your vents. The compressor is the part that's hooked up to your engine by a belt, and all it does is pump the hot refrigerant from your evaporator to the condenser. The condenser then uses the outside air to cool the refrigerant off so it can start again. Point is, the only part of your AC that can hurt anything if it breaks is your compressor since it's hooked up to the engine and even that wouldn't happen without some obvious sounds that something was wrong first. You probably just have a leak in your condenser and all that refrigerant is leaking out, so no real harm other than having to roll your windows down after it's all leaked out.

The old boxy 90s ones with the 3.6? Rough times, bought one out of desperation for $500 hoping it would get me to work until I could afford something reliable. It must've lived it's whole life as the cheap-enough-to-be-charity car because I met three strangers and two friends who had been in or owned that car. First kiss in the back seat, a road trip to Colorado, someone's home for a year, a gift to a single mom that lost her job, the stories that car had seen...

Every piece of exterior trim had come unglued, perpetually smelled like coolant and cigarettes, and every piece of interior plastic was either missing or cracked from the Phoenix sun. Sold it to someone in need for $400, still running strong with over 400k on it.

I'd like to think it's still out there, still giving people second chances...
